title: Should a client build, partner or buy to get into a new market?
description: Build, partner or buy? for case interviews. How to get into a new market or capability. A checklist, a worked example and how to say it.
hook: When a client wants a new capability or a way into a new market, there are three routes: build it, partner for it, or buy it. Here is a simple comparison you can talk through in a case.
body:
When it helps

How to get into a new market or capability.

The comparison

RouteGood becauseWatch out for
Build (organic)Full control; no integration or culture clashSlow; needs skills the client may not have
Partner (JV, alliance)Shared risk and cost; fast accessShared control and profit
Buy (acquire)Fastest; brings customers and skillsExpensive; integration and culture risk

An example

A UK supermarket wants to offer pharmacy services. Build: hire pharmacists and fit out counters. Slow, but full control. Partner: let an existing pharmacy chain run counters inside its stores. Fast and low risk, but the profit is shared. Buy: acquire a pharmacy chain. Fastest, but expensive and hard to integrate. Which is best depends on how fast they need it and how much they want to own the customer relationship.

How it sounds in an interview

There are three ways in: build it, partner for it, or buy it. I'd choose based on speed, cost and how much control we need. Can I check how quickly the client wants this?

A decision with comparable economics

A retailer needs a recommendation engine within twelve months. Building internally costs £2.5 million upfront and £600,000 a year to operate. Buying a specialist business costs £8 million and requires integration. Partnering with an existing vendor costs £1 million a year plus implementation, but may restrict control over data and features.

Compare the options on a consistent horizon. Over three years, the build option costs approximately £4.3 million before financing or opportunity cost; the partnership fees total £3 million before integration; the acquisition price is not the same thing as a three-year expense because the purchased business may retain value. These are illustrative assumptions.

Ask three decisive questions: is the capability competitively differentiating, how urgently is it needed, and can the client actually execute the chosen route? A cheap build that takes two years fails a twelve-month launch. An acquisition that the client cannot integrate may be the riskiest option. Finish by specifying what information could change your answer.
